tier_reason: Benchmark code is public (bench/<case>/<case>.js run by bench/bench.mjs, 5 warm-up runs then median of 21 timed runs, checksum-verified), and bench/results.json meta states CPU (Apple M4 Max), versions (node v25.9.0, clang 19.1.6, asc 0.28.19, jz 0.9.2) and every target's invocation and flags; the bench README's aggregate table gives jz/V8 0.42x and jz/AssemblyScript 0.45x.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'Faster than V8 and AssemblyScript on almost every kernel we measure, about 2x on average'. bench/README.md aggregate geomean table (JZ/target, lab rows excluded): V8 (node) 0.42x, AssemblyScript 0.45x speed. Committed bench/results.json (Apple M4 Max, Node v25.9.0, dated 2026-09-30): geometric mean of per-case median time ratios jz/V8 0.425 over 53 non-lab checksum-ok cases (faster on 52), 0.443 over 55 when the watr/jessie self-compile lab rows are included (about 2.3x faster); jz/AssemblyScript 0.448 over 50 cases (faster on 44); jz run under wasmtime 0.498 of V8 over 52 cases (derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: From bench/results.json meta: V8 = node v25.9.0 running node run-v8.mjs <case>.js; AssemblyScript 0.28.19 = asc <case>.as.ts -O3 (--runtime stub per bench README); jz 0.9.2 = compile(src, { optimize: 'speed' }) run on node's V8 Wasm engine; native references clang 19.1.6 -O3 -march=native -ffp-contract=off and rustc -C opt-level=3 -C target-cpu=native. Each case does 5 warm-up runs and reports the median of 21 timed runs.
corrections.caveats: Compares compiled-to-Wasm code against V8 running the same JS on numeric kernels chosen by the author, with the project's own harness; ratios here are geometric means from results.json rows with parity 'ok' (the bench page jz.js.org was not opened). V8 loses mostly because of dynamic-typing overhead the JS subset removes, not because Wasm is a faster VM; V8 still wins the self-compile lab rows (watr, jessie) and the dynamic-JS deopt probes. results.json is flagged partial: mixed vintages (most jz rows measured at commit e36aab3b, most V8 rows carried from an earlier run) with timing anchors passing within 10%, but the host reported 25,065 MB swap use, above the project's own 4,096 MB claims-gate limit, so the project's own release gate would not accept this snapshot as release evidence. AssemblyScript ports use unchecked() array access while jz keeps bounds checks. Native clang -O3 still leads jz by about 1.2x geomean. The harness records a per-case verdict and treats rows within 1.05x as a tie.

notes: Numbers reproduce exactly from bench/results.json (0.443 over 55, 0.448 over 50, wasmtime lane 0.498 over 52); the page's own aggregate excludes lab rows (0.42x V8). Shortcomings: author-chosen kernels, partial mixed-vintage dataset on a host above the project's own swap limit, V8 still faster on self-compile and deopt-probe rows.

tier_reason: Independent third-party suite (ziyadedher/evm-bench, public benchmark and runner code) whose README table shows revm 84.8 ms vs Geth 235 ms summed over five Solidity workloads; no CPU, toolchain versions or flags are stated, so not A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: revm runner launched with cargo run -r (release profile defaults); Geth runner launched with go run (Go 1.19 module); CPU, toolchain versions and runner versions used for the 2022-12-17 table are not stated.
corrections.caveats: Third-party suite (evm-bench by Ziyad Edher, GPL-3.0, 225 stars) with public code but no CPU, compiler flags or runner versions on the README. The results table was last updated 2022-12-17 (README commit 'Update benchmark times') and the repo's last commit is 2024-03-19 (dependency bumps), so the numbers are close to four years old; the Geth runner pins go-ethereum v1.10.25 and the current revm runner pins revm-interpreter at git rev 3fda52e, while the revm version behind the 2022 table is not recorded. The runners measure different scopes: the current revm runner times the bare revm Interpreter against a DummyHost, while the Geth runner times evm.Call against a state database, so host and state overhead is not equal across rows. evmone, the C++ EVM, is faster still at 66 ms (revm takes 1.285x evmone's time) and is already catalogued; this entry is the revm-versus-Geth evidence.

notes: Numbers match the evm-bench README exactly (revm 84.8 ms, Geth 235 ms, about 2.8x derived). Shortcomings: table dated 2022-12-17 with old Geth v1.10.25, no hardware or versions, asymmetric runners (revm bare interpreter with DummyHost vs Geth evm.Call with state), evmone faster; baseline Geth is not one of the category's listed baselines.

tier_reason: Independent measurement by Frank Denis (libsodium author, not affiliated with Wasmer) with public benchmark code (libsodium dist/wasm32-wasi.sh --bench) and raw per-runtime CSVs; the 2022-12 edition states no CPU model, runtime versions or flags, so not A.

corrections.caveats: Ratios are derived from the raw per-benchmark CSVs (wasmer-llvm.csv, wasmtime.csv, node.csv; values are libsodium's per-iteration times from test/default/cmptest.h, lower is better) in the author's benchmark repo (ISC, archived 2026-08-19), geometric mean over 69 shared rows. The 2022-12 folder has no README; the matching post (00f.net, 2023-01-04, blocked here, snippet only) says the runs used a Zen 2 CPU pinned to one core with each test run 200 times, but no exact CPU model, runtime versions or flags are reachable. Compile time is not part of the measured numbers (LLVM compile is far slower). In the same dataset WAMR's iwasm, a listed baseline, beats wasmer-llvm: wasmer-llvm takes 1.277x iwasm's time (faster on 1 of 69) and 1.171x wasm2c's time (faster on 10 of 70) (derived from page data), and the 2023 post (snippet only) names iwasm the top runtime; so wasmer-llvm beats Wasmtime and V8 but not WAMR AOT on this workload. The 2021-Q1 README by the same author ranked WAVM about 15% ahead of wasmer-llvm. Snippets of the author's 2026 posts (blocked) say Wasmer was the best performer with WAVM, WAMR and Wasmtime close, and that wasm2c used 0.887x Wasmer's time and 0.814x Wasmtime's (Wasmer about 8% faster than Wasmtime, derived from snippet data); not checked on the page. The win is specific to the LLVM backend (wasmer-cranelift ties Wasmtime at 1.02x, singlepass is 3.12x slower) and to this crypto-heavy workload. LICENCE WARNING: the repo root is MIT, but lib/compiler-llvm/LICENSE and lib/compiler-singlepass/LICENSE are Business Source License 1.1 for Wasmer LLVM/Singlepass 6.0.0 or later, with production use allowed only for Wasmer sponsors (change date four years after publication, change licence MPL 2.0); the December 2022 numbers were measured on the older MIT-era LLVM backend. Wasmer is itself a named baseline; this entry is evidence that its LLVM backend beats Wasmtime's default and V8 on steady-state throughput.

notes: Derived geomeans reproduce exactly from the CSVs (0.872 vs wasmtime on 69 rows, faster on 54; 0.747 vs node, faster on 60; cranelift 1.019; singlepass 3.119). Main shortcomings: WAMR iwasm (listed baseline) and wasm2c are faster than wasmer-llvm in the same data, no hardware or versions for the 2022-12 edition, fast backend now BUSL-1.1. The record's statement that the 2026 post puts Wasmtime ahead of Wasmer conflicts with the snippets I saw (Wasmer best, Wasmtime close); I replaced it in caveats.
